topIssues.title: op-node,op-batcher: count L1 confirmations from a configurable block tag (Fast Confirmation Rule)
topIssues.author: krlosMata
topIssues.body:
## Problem

op-node and op-batcher always count their L1 confirmations from the L1 head (`latest`):

- `--verifier.l1-confs`: derivation reads L1 only up to `latest - N` (`op-node/rollup/confdepth/conf_depth.go`).
- `--sequencer.l1-confs`: the sequencer picks its L1 origin up to `latest - N`.
- `--num-confirmations` (op-batcher, via `op-service/txmgr`): a batch tx is confirmed when `tx block + N - 1 <= latest` (`txmgr.queryReceipt`).

A fixed block count is only a guess at reorg safety. Ethereum's Fast Confirmation Rule (FCR) lets a consensus client report a `safe` block that trails `latest` by about one slot and will not be reorged under the rule's assumptions. Today an operator who wants that guarantee has two bad options: keep a large count (slow), or lower it to 1–2 (fast, but no actual safety guarantee). Neither component can express "N blocks below the safe block".

## Proposal

Add an L1 block tag that the existing counts are measured from:

| Component | New flag | Values | Effect |
| :-: | :-: | :-: | :-: |
| op-node | `--verifier.l1-block-tag` | latest (default), safe, finalized | `--verifier.l1-confs` counted from that block |
| op-node | `--sequencer.l1-block-tag` | latest (default), safe, finalized | `--sequencer.l1-confs` counted from that block |
| op-batcher (txmgr) | `--num-confirmations-block-tag` | latest (default), safe, finalized | `--num-confirmations` counted from that block |

The defaults keep today's behaviour. With FCR, `--verifier.l1-block-tag=safe --verifier.l1-confs=0` derives up to the safe block, and `--num-confirmations-block-tag=safe --num-confirmations=1` treats a batch as confirmed once it is in the safe block.

Note: op-node refreshes the L1 safe/finalized blocks every `--l1.epoch-poll-interval` (default 384s). Operators using `safe` with FCR should lower it (e.g. one slot).

## Context

We run OP Stack chains (op-succinct validity proofs) whose downstream components already anchor to the L1 `safe` block. op-node and op-batcher are the remaining components that can only count from `latest`. Draft PRs follow.

topIssues.title: kona-sp1-proposer: resolve foreign ancestors blocking refund claims
topIssues.author: wwared
topIssues.body:
## Summary

Follow up to #22835. A proposer-created game can be blacklisted or retired and therefore eligible to recover its creation bond through refund mode, but resolving that game may still be blocked by an unresolved foreign ancestor.

PR #22835 intentionally does not add permissionless foreign-game resolution. It keeps refund recovery narrow: the proposer resolves and claims only its own disallowed games, and waits when an ancestor has not reached a resolvable state.

## Desired behavior

When an owned disallowed game is blocked by foreign ancestors, identify the minimal unresolved ancestor chain and permissionlessly resolve only ancestors whose on-chain clocks/status make resolution valid. Once the dependency is resolved, continue resolving the owned game and claim its refund-mode credit.

## Constraints

- Do not resolve active or otherwise unready foreign games.
- Preserve parent-before-child transaction ordering across cycles.
- Do not retain foreign games for bond claims or treat them as proposer-owned.
- Keep failures isolated so one foreign dependency does not block unrelated refund claims.
- Avoid a full-history startup scan.

## Acceptance criteria

- A scenario test covers an owned blacklisted/retired game blocked by a resolvable foreign ancestor.
- The foreign ancestor resolves before the owned game.
- The owned game's creation bond is subsequently unlocked and paid through refund mode.
- Unready foreign ancestors produce no resolution transaction.

Filed by an AI coding assistant at the user's request.

topIssues.title: op-deployer: interop and super-root games still gated by devFeatureBitmap in v0.9.0-dev-test.2
topIssues.author: jelias2
topIssues.body:
## Expectation

With the v0.9.0 contracts, interop and super-root games are part of the release. A fresh deployment should therefore not need `devFeatureBitmap` bits `0x1` (`OPTIMISM_PORTAL_INTEROP`) and `0x10000000` (`SUPER_ROOT_GAMES_MIGRATION`) in `globalDeployOverrides`.

The `op-deployer/v0.9.0-dev-test.1` changelog also says: "devfeatures: Enable super root games migration by default (#21689)".

## Actual

All of the following is at tag `op-deployer/v0.9.0-dev-test.2`:

- `op-deployer/pkg/deployer/pipeline/l2genesis.go`: `buildDevFeatureBitmap` returns `interop feature in devFeatureBitmap does not match the UseInterop intent flag` when `useInterop=true` and bit `0x1` is absent.
- `packages/contracts-bedrock/scripts/L2Genesis.s.sol` still gates `CrossL2Inbox`, `L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger`, `ETHLiquidity`, `SuperchainETHBridge` and `UndeliveredMessageExporter` on `OPTIMISM_PORTAL_INTEROP` (`Predeploys.assertGates`).
- `packages/contracts-bedrock/scripts/deploy/DeployImplementations.s.sol` only deploys the `SuperFaultDisputeGame` / `SuperPermissionedDisputeGame` implementations when either bit is set, and asserts they are absent otherwise.
- `OPContractsManagerV2.sol` (around line 753) reads `isDevFeatureEnabled(SUPER_ROOT_GAMES_MIGRATION)` to decide super-root mode in `deploy`; `OPContractsManagerStandardValidator.sol` (around line 951) does the same.

Net effect: without `0x10000000`, an interop chain cannot be deployed with `respectedGameType` 5 or 9 at genesis.

## Impact

- Devnet tooling (netchef in `devnets-private`) must keep passing both bits for every interop / super-root network.
- A user who reads "interop is included" in v0.9.0 and omits the bitmap gets a late failure at L2 genesis, after the L1 contracts have already been broadcast, or a non-interop genesis if the check is bypassed.
- Example network: devnets-private PR #2317 (`int-sr-0`).

## Ask

Either:

1. Default these two bits on (or remove the gates) in op-deployer v0.9.0, so an intent with `useInterop=true` deploys the interop predeploys and super-root games without a bitmap; or
2. Document in the v0.9.0 release notes that the bitmap remains required, and which bits.

---
Filed by Claude Code on behalf of jelias2

topPRs.title: op-chain-ops: add SDM RPC replay checks to check-lagoon
topPRs.author: nonsense
topPRs.body:
Adds read-only SDM RPC validation through `check-lagoon sdm rpc`, with opt-in checks for existing workflows via `--sdm.check-rpc`. Covers debug/parity replay, call-many, transaction-boundary roots, `traceChain`, JS, OTS, and raw/bad-block diagnostics against canonical receipts and state.

JS runs when available; its explicit disabled-tracer response is skipped unless `--sdm.rpc-js` requires it. OTS calls are skipped unless `--sdm.rpc-ots` is set. Unexpected errors and incorrect results still fail. JSON reports distinguish failures from skips; missing fixtures or optional skips leave `complete: false` without failing otherwise successful checks.

Targeted race tests, vet, custom lint, and the op-geth ratchet pass. Default and explicit-required modes were exercised against premium and stock nodes. This is replay-focused coverage, not every RPC/tracer option. Independent review, full-repository lint, and an end-to-end pass against settled-replay release artifacts remain pending.

topPRs.title: kona-gossip,kona-rpc!: Enforce peer, address and subnet blocks on inbound and existing connections
topPRs.author: aakoshh
topPRs.body:
### What

kona-node now enforces the operator's peer, address and subnet blocks, and score bans, on inbound connections and on connections that are already open, not only on its own dials. `opp2p_connectPeer` and `opp2p_disconnectPeer` now wait for the result and report why a connection fails.

### Why

Before this PR, a block only stopped kona's own dials. A blocked peer, or a peer at a blocked address, could still dial in, and an open connection stayed open after its peer was blocked. A score ban disconnected the peer, but nothing kept it from reconnecting at once.

For operators:
- **Blocks** (`opp2p_blockPeer`, `opp2p_blockAddr`, `opp2p_blockSubnet`) refuse inbound connections, by address before the handshake, and close existing connections in both directions. They also apply to protected and static peers. op-node, by contrast, leaves open connections in place. A block that covers a static peer is logged as a warning.
- **Score bans** (`--p2p.ban.peers`) refuse the peer in both directions until the ban expires. As in op-node, `opp2p_unblockPeer` lifts a ban, and bans aren't listed by `opp2p_listBlockedPeers`.
- **`opp2p_connectPeer`** used to fail at once with "Peer not connected" for any peer, because its poll never retried. It now waits up to 30 seconds for the connection, as op-node does, fails at once with the gate's reason for a blocked or banned peer, and returns the dial's error when the dial fails. **`opp2p_disconnectPeer`** waits for the connections to close. Both return only once the P2P RPC's state shows the change, so an `opp2p_peers` call right after lists it. The devstack's `connectL2CLPeers` relies on that.
- **RPC errors:** these two methods' failures now use code `-32000` with the reason, as op-node's do, where they used `-32602` (invalid params) with "Peer not connected" or "Peers are still connected". An address that names no peer, or has nothing to dial before its `/p2p/<peer id>`, is still `-32602`, with a message saying which.
- **`opp2p_peers`** reports `latency` in nanoseconds, as op-node does. It was in whole seconds, so always `0`.
- **The `payload_by_number` sync protocol is no longer served.** op-node retired both its client and its server. kona's stub read each request without a size limit or timeout, so a peer could stream bytes into the node until it ran out of memory.
- **Metrics:** `kona_node_gossip_inbound_connections_refused` is new, by `reason`. `kona_node_dial_peer_error{type="already_connected"}` now counts less, since `opp2p_connectPeer` to a connected peer no longer dials.
- **Logs:** peers connecting and disconnecting are logged at debug, no longer at info and warn. A gossip listener that closes while the node runs is logged as an error.
- **The P2P RPC** answers from gossip state up to a second old. What a command changes shows at once, and so do connection, identify, subscription and address changes. If the network actor doesn't publish fresher state within two seconds, a call answers from the last state.

Closes #23715. Closes #23701.

### How

- **The blocks live in `gate::Behaviour`, a `NetworkBehaviour`,** the first field of the gossip `Behaviour`. The swarm asks its behaviours about a connection in `handle_pending_inbound_connection`, before the handshake, and in `handle_established_*_connection`, once the peer ID is known. These are the only points where a connection can be refused. By the time the driver sees `ConnectionEstablished`, gossipsub has already queued its subscriptions, so the driver could only close the connection again. Being the first field means the gate is asked before gossipsub, identify and ping.
- **`ConnectionGater` keeps only the dial bookkeeping,** and checks the gate it is given. The gater's write-only `connectedness` map is gone (#23701).
- **The RPC's gossip snapshot is built on demand.** The network actor used to rebuild it after every step: for each gossip message, ping and identify event. It now publishes after each command, and when a reader asks for one fresher than the reader's `max_age`, through a refresh channel with room for one request, so readers that ask at the same time share one build. It also publishes when the swarm reports a change the snapshot shows.
- **`ConnectPeer` and `DisconnectPeer` carry a reply,** which the driver answers from the swarm event that settles the outcome. `ConnectPeer` carries a `PeerAddr`, so the RPC parses the address once. A refusal by the gate, before the dial or once the connection is established, comes back typed, as `ConnectPeerError::Refused`.
- **`GossipDriver::start` returns a `PeerAddr`,** which always ends in the node's peer ID.
- **The devstack's `TestP2PPeers`** expected a blocked peer to stay connected, as in op-node. On kona nodes, it now waits for the connection to close, and reconnects the peer after unblocking it.

### Caveats

- A peer refused by its peer ID still completes the Noise handshake, since the ID is only known after it. op-node's `InterceptSecured` works the same way. Address and subnet blocks refuse before the handshake.
- A static peer given by a DNS name can't be matched against an address block until it is connected, so the warning about blocking it may not appear.
- Blocks and bans don't survive a restart (#23768).
- Scores and ping latencies in RPC answers can be up to a second old, since they change without an event.
- A gossip listener that closes while the node runs is logged, but the node keeps running without it (#23793).
- op-node versions that still run the sync request client get "protocol not supported" from kona now, and may score it down. That client has been off by default since #18088, and was removed in op-node v1.19.1.
- The `opp2p_*` methods are served to anyone who can reach the RPC port, which listens on `0.0.0.0` by default, as in op-node. Blocks are stronger now, so `opp2p_blockSubnet 0.0.0.0/0` cuts the node off from every peer (#23798).
- The gossip peerstore keeps every peer that ever completed identify. This PR also stops removing a banned peer's entry, for parity with op-node (#23800).

### Alternatives

- **The blocklist as shared state in the driver** (`Arc<RwLock>`): rejected, because the driver only sees a connection after it is established, and can't refuse it before.
- **Bounding the sync stub instead of removing it:** done first, in its own commit (read exactly the 8-byte request, with op-node's 10-second deadline), then removed, since op-node no longer uses the protocol.
- **Dialing an unblocked static peer at once:** rejected. `opp2p_connectPeer` covers the urgent case, and the driver would have needed another way to schedule its checks. The peer is dialed at the next check, within a minute.
- **Listing score bans in `opp2p_listBlockedPeers`:** rejected, for parity with op-node, and because a tool that copies blocks between nodes would turn temporary bans into permanent blocks. Making bans visible is #23796.

- **Dropping `test_sync_request_protocol_is_unsupported` once the protocol was gone,** as a review suggested: kept, so that a peer asking for the protocol is shown to get "protocol not supported", rather than a stream kona never answers.

### Potential follow-ups

- Split `kona-gossip/src/driver.rs`, now about 2,000 lines, into a module by concern, as a pure move.
- Move the JSON-RPC wire types (`PeerInfo`, `PeerDump`, ...) from `kona-gossip` to `kona-rpc`, or to an RPC-types crate.
- Make `GossipDriver` generic over its message handler. Today it knows OP payload types, the v1–v4 block topics and the signer rotation, and takes the chain ID from the block handler's rollup config.
- `NetworkActor::step` is hard to read and to test as one `select!`. The `next`/`handle` split proposed in #23534 and #23580 would help, for example for #23793.
- Filed: #23793 (stop the node when the gossip listener closes), #23796 (show score bans over the RPC, and the misleading `banned*` field names), #23797 (late blocks from the previous signer are rejected at a signer rotation), #23798 (don't serve the P2P control methods to anyone who can reach the RPC port), #23800 (prune disconnected peers from the peerstore), #23768 (keep blocks and bans across restarts, now with a startup warning about blocked static peers).

BREAKING CHANGE: Rust users of `kona-gossip` and `kona-rpc` need to update their code; the node's command-line flags and RPC methods don't change.
- The sync request/response protocol is gone, with `Behaviour::sync_req_resp`, `GossipDriverBuilderError::{SetupSyncReqRespError, SyncReqRespAlreadyAccepted}` and `Event::Stream`.
- `GossipDriver`'s `swarm`, `addr`, `handler` and `peerstore` fields are private, and `behaviour_mut` is gone. Use `addr()`, `handler()`, `peer_addr()`, `connected_peers()` (now the peer IDs, not a count), and the driver's `block_*`, `unblock_*` and `list_blocked_*` methods.
- `ConnectionGater`'s blocklist and `connectedness` fields, and the `ConnectionGate` trait's block, list and `connectedness` methods, are gone; `ConnectionGate::can_dial` takes the `gate::Behaviour`.
- `GossipDriver::start` returns a `PeerAddr`; `dial_peer` and `dial_multiaddr` return a `Result`.
- `GossipCommand::ConnectPeer` carries a `PeerAddr` named `peer` and a reply sender, and `DisconnectPeer` a reply sender. `GossipDriver::connect_peer` takes a `PeerAddr`.
- `NetworkActorError::DriverStartup` is gone; nothing returned it.
- `GossipQueryHandle::new` takes the refresh sender, and `GossipQueryHandle::snapshot` is async and takes the oldest snapshot age the caller accepts. `GossipState::pings` is a field.

topPRs.title: op-zk-proposer: local CUDA proof provider and op-zk-proposer-cuda image
topPRs.author: Inphi
topPRs.body:
Adds `OP_ZK_PROPOSER_PROOF_PROVIDER=local-cuda`, a self-hosted backup for an SPN outage (ethereum-optimism/proofs-team#51). Proofs come from SP1's `sp1-gpu-server`, one per CUDA device, through the existing request/wait flow. A new amd64 image, `op-zk-proposer-cuda`, adds the server, the CUDA 12.8 runtime, and the v6.1.0 PLONK circuits to the existing binary.

The proposer starts each server itself and speaks the public `sp1_cuda::api` socket protocol, instead of using the SP1 SDK's CUDA client, which downloads a missing or mismatched server from GitHub at runtime. A startup `--version` check keeps the server and the protocol types on the linked SP1 version, and the server gets no `OP_ZK_PROPOSER_*` variables.

A CPU pre-execution enforces the cycle and memory limits before a request reaches a GPU and classifies failures as SPN does, so bisection and chain splitting work unchanged. Other local failures are resubmitted. A broken GPU server connection exits the process, so every server stops and the pod restarts; local proof progress is in memory and is lost. Network and mock mode do not change. The README's "Local CUDA proving" section covers sizing, `/dev/shm`, and known limits (queued stdin memory, no hung-server detection, no release tag for the CUDA image).

Testing: unit tests drive the provider through a scripted GPU server and executor, and the socket client against a fake server. No real GPU proof has run, and this PR's CI is the first melange/apko build of the new image.

topPRs.body:
Merges `proposal/op-contracts/v9.0.0` into develop, bringing the Glamsterdam support fixes that were built on the proposal branch and didnt land previously on develop.

Conflicts take develop's side, except L1CrossDomainMessenger, which keeps develop's interop functions and adds the proposal's relay gas constants. L1CrossDomainMessenger and OptimismPortal2 move past develop's versions to `3.2.0` and `7.2.0`. The semver lock and upgrade bundle are regenerated in a separate commit, and `git show --remerge-diff 5dd5a92216` shows only the resolutions. Genesis now ships a newer L2CrossDomainMessenger than the frozen Lagoon bundle, so Lagoon needs a re-snapshot after this lands.

topPRs.title: docs: List code that gas repricings can affect
topPRs.author: ajsutton
topPRs.body:
Adds a list of the code that a gas repricing on L1 or L2 can affect, in ways other than cost. The list covers gas introspection, fixed gas limits for calls, transactions, and deposits, copies of gas schedules, and gas limit bounds. Production, deployment-only, and test code are in separate sections.

A fork that changes gas costs can break these sites without a compile error, for example the `CrossL2Inbox` warm read check or the fixed gas limits of upgrade deposits. Without a list, each fork must find these sites again. The document tells readers to add new cases when they find them. There is no effect on users.

Search agents built the list and a separate review agent checked it. I applied all its findings. The test section groups repeated cases by file and does not list each line.
